TrackAStory
A planner moves the story alpha through its statuses, records a conflict in its criteria, replaces the conflict
    with another, and clears it. They mark it Done with spaces around the word and Blocked: waiting with tabs around it, and the story keeps the words alone.
    A second story keeps its own status throughout.

ReshapeThePlan
A planner grows the plan and trims it. They create a fourth epic, give it a story, retitle and relink the first
    epic's stories, find where a story and its spec live and which branch it takes, delete a story, and delete the
    new epic, which a story can no longer be filed under, and the second epic. They name the new epic by its
    slug and by an old NNNN-slug name, because the book cannot know the id the tool minted.

UnblockStories
A planner finds stories a run gave up on and sets them going again. They unblock one story and then an epic's,
    unblock a story that is not blocked, set two stories aside again and unblock every story to a status of their own
    choosing, and find unblock refusing a call that names nothing, two scopes or something that is not there.

ReadThePlan
A planner looks at the plan and changes nothing. They check its integrity, list its epics and stories, search it,
    build the index, ask which epic and which story come next and which stories cover a seed, read the checks a QA plan
    may use, preview a rename, and ask the stack commands what they hold. The files stay as they were.

ReadABook\nA reviewer opens a small book. They check it, rewrite its index, search it, explain one endpoint and a name it\n    lacks, list its decisions and its book pages, walk its model, draw its state graph and run its journeys against the app.

RunAQaPlan
A reviewer checks a QA plan and runs it. They lint and validate a plan that is sound and one that is not, run
    both, read the report, the replay and the ledger before and after a run, find that nothing was recorded on video,
    then open a session by hand, record a step and an assertion, and close it.

TryWhatTheSandboxLacks
A reviewer reaches for what a text sandbox does not hold. They validate a plan for a browser and one for a phone,
    try to run both and find the run blocked on a secret before anything starts, run a plan that calls a gRPC service
    nobody serves and see it fail, bring up a book with no stack, and ask the visual check for nothing, for a regions
    file that is not there, for a story that does not exist, and for a clean dry run.

A planner writes the documents around the plan. They open a milestone, list its epics and the backlog items it owns,
    file a record on the Register and close it, file a decision, type a story's spec and scaffold its artifact, and declare

A rule that sits above any one service has no decision to live in, because a decision must name elements of one
service's book. Such a rule goes in a page of one of three books, by how far it reaches. The product book is
`products/<product>/<slug>.md` in the artifacts dir: the product's own words, a constraint no story may break and the place where the
truth for a calculation lives. The team book is `teams/<team>/<slug>.md` in the artifacts dir: how one team builds
across products, as ADRs, RFCs and conventions. The company book is `company/<slug>.md` in the artifacts dir: the rules
every team follows. Agents write product pages. People write team and company pages.
The product is `book.product` in the code repository's `agents.yml`, else the repository's name. With `book.home: repo`
the product book stays `product/<slug>.md` beside `services/`. Started in the artifacts folder, `book pages` lists every
product folder under `products/`, and a product page's search heading is `== product <name>`.
The team is `book.team` in the code repository's `agents.yml`, else in the manifest found from the book root. With no `book.team` the team book is not read, and another
team's folder is never read. A folder that does not exist is skipped without a word.
A page has a `date:` line, an optional `sources:` line naming who said it or where it is written, an optional `status:`
line of free text such as proposed, accepted or superseded by another slug, a blank line, then prose whose first line is
its statement. It names no story and no element.
When two books disagree, the order of authority is company, team, product, service decision, story. A reader that finds
a conflict reports it and picks neither side.
`book search` reads the three levels in every case, with a service named or not. It prints their hits before the
service books', under `== company`, `== team <name>` and `== product` (`== product <name>` when the book has a named product), in that order, in the same lines as a decision's.
The kinds `company`, `team` and `product` each show only that level and every other kind leaves the levels out. A page
whose status starts with superseded is still found, and its hit line ends with `(superseded)`. A book with none of the
folders prints exactly what it printed before.
`book pages` lists one line for each page: the level, the slug, the date, the status when there is one and the
statement. `--level` keeps one level. With `--check` it prints each page with no `date:` line or an empty body and
exits 1, else exits 0. It takes no service because a page belongs to none. The sandbox's small book holds no page, so
the book sees the command exit 0 and no more.

What a story plays is bounded by construction.
A story plays three ranks. Rank 1 is the journeys whose own class the change added or edited. Rank 2 is the calls whose
own class the change added or edited, and the calls of an edited action or screen class. Rank 3 is the calls of the
elements whose `source=` names a changed file or symbol with no hop in between, and of the elements a hunk with no

What the change reaches through a hop, or through a changed shared book definition, is counted under `reached`. That
selection belongs to the scheduled whole play, and a story never plays it.
`only`, `journeys` and `by_journey` keep their content, so the other consumers of the report do not change.
The accepted cost is that a call the change alters through a shared helper is judged only by the scheduled whole play.

`ostler book affected --story <id>` reads the change of one story as its own commits and the uncommitted work, not as
the range from a base commit to the working tree. A commit is the story's when its `Story:` trailer names the id. A
message that only mentions the id in its body is not the story's.
The range made every plan `whole` on trunk. Commits of other work landed between the story's, their symbols were named
by no element, and the exit code 1 of the uncovered list stopped the plays before any service played. Reading only the
story's commits drops that foreign work.
Each file is compared from the parent of the first story commit that touched it to the last story commit that touched
it. The uncommitted and untracked work is read as well, because the seat's new journeys are uncommitted when the
selection runs: a file dirty in the working tree is compared to the working tree from the same start, and a file that is
only dirty is compared from HEAD.
The accepted risk is the span. A foreign commit that edits a file between two story commits that touch the same file
shows its hunks in that file's span, because the span runs from before the first story commit to after the last. The
selection then names a few symbols more than the story wrote. It never names fewer.
With no commit carrying the trailer the command exits 2 and writes no report. It does not fall back to the range,
because the range is what made the selection wrong. The coder reads the commits first and passes `--story` only when
some commit carries the trailer, and otherwise reads the range as before.
The plan keeps the kind `whole` when a fallback applies, and the report adds an `owed` list of the fallback reasons
instead of a new kind. Under `whole`, `only` and `by_journey` are already the selection the walk names, since a record hit and a
fallback add no call. A caller that plays what the selection names and owes the rest reads `owed`. The kinds `none`,
`empty`, `partial` and `whole` and the `reason` field stay as they were, so the coder's merge of kinds and the okf book
workflows that key on `whole` are unchanged.
The book of ostler does not play `affected`. The command reads a git checkout, and the demo world of the book is not
one. A later story can add a separate git world and an element for it.
`stale --story` and `verified --story` read the same commits, committed work only, because `verified` writes HEAD.
`verified --story` refuses only for the story's code, and writes no stamp while other commits leave code unnamed. A stamp
over foreign code with no pointer would hide it from every later reading that starts at the verified commit.

`status of '<story>' cannot be empty` on standard output, exits 1 and writes no file. It lives in
`ostler/ostler/crud.py::set_status`, which the command line and `Ostler.set_status` share, so both refuse alike.
The story lookup runs first. An unknown story keeps its own refusal, `no story with id '<story>'`, whatever the status.
Every other text stays accepted, `Done` and `Blocked: waiting` among them, because the repository names no list of
story statuses. The spaces and tabs around a status are dropped before it is written, and the success line prints
the status without them. Whether a fixed list of statuses should exist stays open, as entry 1 of
`UNDERSPECIFIED.md`.
The book plays the refusal with an empty status, a status of spaces and a status of a tab, each on a known story and
the empty one on an unknown story, and it watches both the frontmatter line and the Implementation Status line so a
refused call is judged to change neither. `Ostler(root).set_status(story, "")` answers a failed result with the same
message; the book reaches the tool through the command line only, so the API half is checked by the story's QA.

Some commands a person types need a machine the sandbox is not: a browser, a phone, a gRPC service, a screenshot or a
running stack. The book declares them, plays the answers the sandbox can produce, and declares the others unseen with
the runtime they need.
`qa run` of a browser plan and of a phone plan is refused before anything starts. The plans read a secret from an
environment variable the sandbox does not set, and the run checks the machine and the secrets first and prints
`QA run blocked:` and one line for each thing missing. A machine without Playwright, ffmpeg, Maestro or adb adds lines to
that list, so the book leaves every line opaque and judges the exit code. A passing run needs a browser or a device and the
secret, and `Unseen(..., Because.RUNTIME, ...)` says so. `qa validate` of both plans passes, because it reads the plan
and starts nothing.
`qa run` of a plan that calls a gRPC service nothing serves runs, and the call fails, so the run answers
`QA run FAILED: 0 assertions passed, 1 failed, 1 scenarios`. The plan names `localhost:1`, where nothing listens, and the
failure is the same with or without `grpcurl` installed. A pass needs a service that answers.
`ostler vet` takes a screenshot, a manifest and either a regions file or a browser address. The book plays the usage
refusal with no arguments, a regions file that is not there and a story that does not exist, and a dry run against a regions
file that lists no region, which is clean and writes nothing. The sandbox holds no image, so the dry run names a screenshot
that does not exist, and the check does not read it when no region asks for a crop. The `--write` path, the `--cdp-url`
scan of a live browser and a report that is not clean are not played.
`ostler env up` of a book with no stack is refused before a container, a lease or a checkout is touched. A bring-up of the
demo book would pull and start an image, and the book does not play that. An earlier pass of this book started one by
mistake and tore it down with `env down`; the image layer stays in the machine's cache.
`ostler env reset` of a copy that was never brought up is refused before a container is touched, and the refusal names
`ostler env up`. A reset of a copy that is up drops its volumes and starts it again, which needs the same image pull
and start the book does not play, so the book plays only the refusal.

`ostler create epic <slug>` mints an id, writes `art/epics/<id>/epic.md` with the id, the slug, the title and the
status `planned` in its frontmatter, and prints `created epic '<slug>' (<id>)`. `ostler create story` mints an id,
writes `stories/<id>/story.md` and prints `created story '<slug>' (<id>) in epic '<epic>'`. The id is a fresh ULID in
every world, so the book cannot say it, and the folder the command writes carries it.
The book therefore declares those lines opaque, and the watch reads only the folders the sandbox starts with, each by
its id. The model keeps a created epic as a `MintedEpic` by its slug and a created story as a `MintedStory` by its
epic and slug, so the commands that follow answer as the app does: a story filed under the new epic, a second story
with the same slug reported as already there, the new epic's slug refused to a second `create epic`. A story created
under one of the sandbox's epics is read from that epic's page, which gains the story's heading and title.
`create epic` takes a slug. An old `NNNN-slug` name gives the slug alone, so `create epic 0007-seventh` makes the epic
`seventh`. A slug an epic already has is refused with `epic '<slug>' already exists (<folder>)`, and the folder is an
id. The model can name that folder only for the epics the sandbox starts with, so no cell creates an epic twice.
`create story` into a slug the epic already holds changes nothing and answers success with
`story '<slug>' already exists in epic '<epic>'`, the epic as typed.
`delete epic` of a created epic prints `deleted epic '<id>'`. `DeleteCreatedEpic` plays that call with the line left
out, and the journey reads the deletion from the `create story` that follows, which the app refuses with
`no epic '<slug>'`. The sandbox's epics are deleted through `DeleteEpic`, whose line the book compares.
A story the book creates has an id no later step can name, so the book never sets its status, deletes it or updates it.
Those commands play on the three stories the sandbox starts with.

elements: Doctor
`ostler doctor` judges only the epics its repo minted. One artifacts dir holds the epics of every repo that shares it,
and each repo mints ids under the `repo.id_prefix` its `agents.yml` sets. An epic whose id carries another prefix
belongs to the repo that minted it. Its milestones and declared fixtures live there, so judging it here would report
`epic-without-milestone` and `unknown-story-fixture` for an epic that is sound in its own repo. Doctor leaves such an
epic out of its findings and its epic list.
`ostler doctor --epic <id>` on an epic another repo minted answers one `foreign-epic` warning. The warning names both
prefixes and tells the reader to run the command from the repo that minted the epic.
An epic whose id carries no prefix stays judged, and so does every epic in a repo that sets no prefix.

The milestones are the one list of the work. ostler keeps no epics queue: no `ostler todo` command, no `index.md` queue
file on the epics shelf and no `epics-todo.json`. A repository that still holds either file keeps it as an ordinary file
that ostler never reads.
`Ostler.milestone_epics` gives every epic a milestone lists, once. A milestone's `dependsOn` milestones come first, and
each milestone gives its epics in the order its `epics:` list holds them. A superseded milestone gives no epics.
`next-epic` prints the first of them with unfinished work.
A shared queue let one run's progress change what every other run and every person saw. The coder worked the front of
the queue and committed each finished epic's removal, so two runs on one repository raced over one file. A run now keeps
what it finished on its own worklist, and the milestones change only when a person edits them.

which imports `os` and claims coverage no check binds. The sound plan has one scenario on a `cli` target with the
`fixture` mechanism and one check that does not touch a process, a network or a browser. A plan with a `live` mechanism,
a daemon, a Playwright or Maestro target, or a recording is not played, so `qa frames` is only ever refused, and the
files under `ostler/ostler/qa/harness/` that drive a browser or a device stay open in `QUESTIONS.md`.

`validate` and `run` alike. The unbound claim in the same plan would be refused by the validation, and the book does
not play it apart.

removes the session file, which the cell `run the plan` in the open scene shows. `qa report` writes the report when the
spec has a ledger and refuses when it has none. `qa stop` prints how many assertions passed and always `0 steps`, because
the step count the stop prints is the live-mechanism steps. `qa step` runs its command and records it, and the book plays

sources: core/stablemate_core/books.py::book_home, ostler/ostler/book/index.py::book_root, core/stablemate_core/book_branch.py, ostler/ostler/book/home.py
A book lives in the artifacts folder unless the repository says otherwise. `ostler book` resolves its book root through
one function of the shared core, `book_home`, and no command walks up from the working directory looking for a
`services/` folder.
A repository that sets `book: {home: repo}` in its `agents.yml` keeps its book beside its code. The nearest `agents.yml`
at or above the working directory decides, and the walk stops at the repository top, so a fixture folder with its own
`agents.yml` is its own book root. A repository with no key reads its book in the artifacts folder. A start inside the
artifacts folder, or inside a worktree of the artifacts repository, reads that checkout. A start in a worktree of the
code on a branch reads the artifacts worktree on the same branch when one exists, and the artifacts folder otherwise.
A repository that still holds an ostler book where the artifacts folder is now the home is refused. The refusal is a
`service.py` at `services/<name>/` or `services/<name>/<surface>/` whose text imports `ostler.book`, in a repository whose
`agents.yml` does not keep the book. The command exits 2 and names both ways out: set `book: {home: repo}`, or move the
book to the artifacts folder with the guide. A `services/` folder that holds no ostler book, such as an application's own
`services/user/service.py`, is not refused.
A source pointer written `repo://<name>/<path>` resolves for a lone repository, from the repository itself or from
`--app`. The name is the repository's name, as for a member of a workspace. A bare pointer resolves against `--app`.
Stablemate and the sandbox keep their book through `book.home: repo`. The sandbox also holds `unmoved/`, a repository
with an ostler book and no key, so the book plays the refusal.
A book change is committed in the artifacts repository on a branch with the same name as the code branch of the same
work. For a story that is the story's branch. A book branch always lives in a linked worktree of the artifacts
repository, and the artifacts folder itself never leaves its base branch, so two pieces of work in two repositories
never switch one shared checkout. The book branch lands on the artifacts base when the code lands on its base, by
rebase and fast-forward, never a merge commit. A change with no code branch, committed straight on the code's base,
commits its book straight on the artifacts base. With `book.home: repo` there is no book branch: the book rides the
code's branch.
`ostler book branch` opens the book branch for the current code branch and prints the book root. `ostler book land`
lands it and removes the worktree and the branch. A conflict keeps both and names the files. The book does not play
`branch` and `land`, because the demo world is not a git checkout, as for `affected` (see
`a-storys-change-is-its-own-commits.md`).

`App(ignore=...)` names 25 modules of `ostler/ostler/book/`. No command a person types reaches them from a text
sandbox, and none of them holds a command, a subcommand or a flag of its own. They are the runtime the plays of other
books run on:
- The surfaces of web, phone, gRPC and signed-credential books: `browser.py`, `pagesurface.py`, `pagedata.py`,
`listjudge.py`, `screen.py`, `asked.py`, `device.py`, `mobilesurface.py`, `rpc.py`, `proxy.py`, `signed.py` and
`delivery.py`.
- The definitions every kind of book shares, which `ostler book` loads for the book it reads and never calls on a
command book: `arrange.py`, `backstage.py`, `boundary.py`, `cast.py`, `contracts.py`, `denied.py`, `entries.py`,
`errors.py`, `event.py`, `planner.py`, `stack.py`, `surface.py` and `workspace.py`.
The plays of the books that use each surface exercise them: the screen books under the book root drive a browser or a
device through `pagesurface.py`, `browser.py`, `screen.py`, `mobilesurface.py` and `device.py`, the gRPC books through
`rpc.py`, and a book with a Bus or credentials through `delivery.py` and `signed.py`. The ostler book plays a command
book and nothing else, and the `ostler book` commands it plays (`check`, `index`, `search`, `explain`, `decisions`,
`explore`, `run`, `graph`) run only the modules its `source` pointers name.
The ignore lifts when a sandbox can hold a browser, a device, a gRPC server and a bus, or when the book root holds a
second book of ostler's own per surface that these commands run against. Each file then gets an element, and its pattern
leaves `App(ignore=...)`.
`ostler/ostler/api.py` is ignored for the reason in `commands-carry-their-words-in-the-argv.md`: it is the in-process
entry point of workflow nodes, and no command line reaches it.

`ostler unblock` clears the stamp a run leaves on a story, and a status is a stamp when it starts with `Blocked`,
`Docs blocked` or `QA give-up` (`ostler/ostler/select.py::is_blocked`). The book reaches a blocked story with
`set-status ... "Blocked: waiting"`, the one blocked status the watch knows.
The command takes one scope: a story id, `--epic`, or `--all`. It refuses none, two or a story and an epic together,
in that order, and then an unknown story or an unknown epic. A scope with no blocked story answers success with
`nothing to unblock`, and with the name it was given when it names a story or an epic.
The restored status is `Not started` unless `--status` gives another, and the summary prints it as typed, so
`unblock --all --status in-progress` says `-> in-progress`. The stories are listed epic by epic, in the order of the epics' id folders, and each epic's in the order its
page lists them.

Look: `ostler/ostler/book/` holds the runtime of every surface. The sandbox plays a command book, so the modules of the browser, phone, gRPC, proxy and signed-credential surfaces (`browser.py`, `pagesurface.py`, `screen.py`, `pagedata.py`, `listjudge.py`, `asked.py`, `device.py`, `mobilesurface.py`, `rpc.py`, `proxy.py`, `signed.py`, `delivery.py`) and the shared parts no command book calls (`arrange.py`, `backstage.py`, `boundary.py`, `cast.py`, `contracts.py`, `denied.py`, `entries.py`, `errors.py`, `event.py`, `planner.py`, `stack.py`, `surface.py`, `workspace.py`) stay unnamed. Which of them the book names and which it leaves to `App(ignore=...)` is still to settle.

Look: `ostler/ostler/qa/harness/ostler_qa_browser*.py`, `ostler_qa_dom.py`, `ostler_qa_elements.py`, `ostler_qa_grpc.py`, `qa/android.py` and `qa/maestro_sessions.py` run only for a plan with a browser, gRPC or device target, and the sandbox has none. The sound plan the book seeds uses the `cli` target. The harness files that check responses, documents, files, paths, hierarchy, scans, settling, transfers, verdicts and verifiers run only for a plan that reads those, which the seeded plan does not.
Look: `ostler vet` takes a screenshot and a manifest of regions. A sandbox seed holds text only, so the command cannot be played past its refusals until a seed can hold an image.

Look: `ostler env up`, `compose`, and the checkout and lease code (`environments/checkout.py`, `environments/leases.py`) need a container runtime that pulls and starts images, and a checkout of a member repository. The book plays `schema`, `check`, `ls`, `render`, `address`, `down` and `exec`.
UnblockStories: `ostler unblock` calls `set_status` with the story's id and drops a story with no id; the book has no story without an id, so that branch is unplayed.
